topics.title: CancelThisco "who owns everything" reels
topics.what: Fact-checking a series of reels from the same creator, CancelThisco, about big fund firms 'owning' and 'controlling' everything.
topics.summary:
1. Oct 25, about 9:40 AM PT: asked to prove a 'final boss' reel right or wrong and build an easy way to see it.
2. Verdict: misleading. Vanguard, BlackRock and State Street do show up at the top of most big companies, but usually hold under 10% each on behalf of index-fund investors, and the 'final boss' stake behind the reveal was sold by 2011. A clickable ownership map shows a verdict and sources for each of the 10 claims.
3. Oct 25, about 11:02 AM PT: a second reel, 'Control the money, control the world', was also misleading: it strings some real facts into a story they don't support and never actually explains how money is created. It's a second tab on the same page, with verdicts and sources for 20 claims.
4. Oct 25, about 7:02 PM PT: two more videos from the same creator, CancelThisco. Part 2 of 'The million dollar question' is misleading: big funds really do hold most of large US companies, but mostly as savers' index-fund and pension money, not one 'Megacorp'. A longer video about the Wallenberg family, Ericsson and BlackRock's board gets most facts right but inflates the family's size.
5. Oct 26, about 6:52 AM PT: 'Power to the people, Part 1' is misleading too. Its wealth-gap numbers are real, but the claims that the rich 'made it legal to manipulate' the market and that banks are about to collapse are false. It's tab 5, and every button on tabs 3 to 5 was tested.
6. Oct 26 morning, on a call: CancelThisco looks like Ian Carroll's brand (it started as a T-shirt shop). The black, gray and white ownership diagram from Part 2 rests on a stake in BlackRock that was sold in 2011. In his colors, BlackRock today is about 85% other companies, 2% insiders and 13% regular people, with Vanguard the biggest single owner at about 8%.
7. Oct 26, about 7:09 AM PT: asked to stop giving these the benefit of the doubt and check each claim against the worst thing that has really happened before. A 'Worst real case' switch is now on the page: each claim shows its worst real precedent (like LIBOR rigging, the 2008 crash or bank money-laundering cases), tagged as accident, negligence or proven intent, and 12 claims flip to 'this has really happened'.
8. Oct 26 evening: Reels 6 and 7 added. 'The real reason why BlackRock controls so much' is misleading (its bank total counts JPMorgan twice). 'This bank owns 45% of BlackRock' is false at its core: that's the old Merrill Lynch stake, fully sold by June 2011.
9. Oct 26 late night: Reels 8 and 9 added. 'Explaining all the crime GameStop exposed' is misleading (the shorts mostly did close in 2021, per the SEC). 'Probably nothing', which calls itself satire, is misleading, with several false claims about the CIA and the Epstein files.
10. Oct 27 morning: a new Layered ownership view on the page traces the big three's stakes through chains of companies for 38 companies. Following the chains adds only about 1 point on average (about 20% direct, about 21% traced), and even a deliberately overstated worst case never reaches 50%. The stronger point is voting power, not ownership.
11. Oct 27, about 8:33 AM PT: Reels 10 and 11 added with the layered check. 'Support small businesses' (buybacks and CEO pay) is misleading, and 'Health is wealth folks' (seed oils, Harvard and a Hong Kong family) is misleading. The series now covers 11 reels.
topics.leftOff: Oct 27, about 8:33 AM PT: 11 CancelThisco reels checked, with the Worst real case switch and the Layered ownership view live. Waiting on the next one.
